rubric.orientation: The opening asks how ceremonial authority could continue under a government ban.
rubric.explanation: Prosecution, compelled surrender, collection dispersal and construction of cultural centers connect a law with institutional decisions.
rubric.evidence: The center connects suspended sentences to surrender of belongings, documents the dispersal of objects and describes a return conditional on facilities for their care. One shipment cannot account for every object.
rubric.chronology_geography: 1884 legislation, the 1921 gathering, 1951 revision and subsequent returns are separate moments. The report period is distinguished from publication.
rubric.perspective: Community recollections are attributed; the title-page credits for Hunt and Boas answer a different question from community testimony.
rubric.reading: The section on care after return puts storage and decision-making in the foreground, without assigning a full custody history to unidentified belongings.
rubric.activity: Readers can compare title-page credits and dates, then bring a community account to a separate question without performing a ceremony.
rubric.connections: Contrasting prohibition, continuation and community-directed care makes the case comparable while keeping authority attached to particular people.

rubric.orientation: The opening asks what changes when a village is placed roughly a century later.

rubric.evidence: The abstract describes ca.1595–1626 with 95.4% probability while the Discussion calls 1595–1626 the extremes of 68.3% ranges. The audit checked both passages. The display correctly avoids assigning one probability to an exact foundation date.
rubric.chronology_geography: The two calendar possibilities near 1500 and 1600 are distinct from continuous occupation between them or a date for other villages.
rubric.perspective: The recovered Wendat name and community account help interpret family life, which the dating graph cannot show.
rubric.reading: Reworded the editorial instruction about retaining uncertainty as an explanation of why the year the first house was built remains unknown.
rubric.activity: Corrected the panel (b) label spacing. The task directs attention to its separated groups and asks what an additional kind of evidence contributes.
rubric.connections: Comparison with a differently dated site would require its own samples; a shared calendar is not evidence of a meeting.

rubric.orientation: An identifiable treaty and its ratification introduce a question about what would show implementation.
rubric.explanation: An allowance, promised skilled work and reports of cloth distribution illustrate how a commitment can be investigated.
rubric.evidence: Powless attributes concrete preparation to participants, including setting a table, bringing benches and chairs, and preparing food. His account describes custody and participation; it is insufficient to establish implementation of every treaty promise.
rubric.chronology_geography: Signing in November 1794, ratification in January 1795 and the 1989 return belong to separate events.
rubric.perspective: The Nation’s description of the Washington Belt and the later participant’s account are credited separately from the United States ratification.
rubric.reading: Changed a note about the author’s research process into a specific question about tracing the custody of a belt through an inventory and agreement.
rubric.activity: The document labels and cloth example allow a family to name an additional receipt or witness account for one promised action.
rubric.connections: The final question can be applied to comparable treaties while retaining the Nation-specific account and written obligations.

rubric.orientation: The bilingual newspaper opens a question about public voice, political security and unequal participation.
rubric.explanation: Making and financing a paper, printing disputes and the consequences of removal explain both the capacities and limits of print.
rubric.evidence: Boudinot identifies S. Foreman and describes his service and the Council’s lack of provision for a replacement. The letter is marked by its own signature and date on a page also containing editorial material and other correspondence. It is not a payroll or the consensus of readers.
rubric.chronology_geography: The constitution, February first issue, April supplied page and 1832 exchange have separate dates; a later rebuilding period also belongs to the inquiry.
rubric.perspective: The account distinguishes correspondents from editors, and the history of enslavement and Freedmen from general claims of national liberty.
rubric.reading: Deeper reading explains how to identify changes of speaker when one page contains more than one kind of text.
rubric.activity: The masthead can be inspected at its available resolution. The supplied constitutional capsule provides evidence for the separate question about political participation.
rubric.connections: The return to the newspaper distinguishes an observable feature, a promise and an experience that would require another record.

rubric.orientation: A signed proclamation introduces the question of what remained to be done after independence was asserted.
rubric.explanation: Resistance, negotiations and a contested federal settlement explain why 1945, 1949 and 1950 denote different changes.
rubric.evidence: The Dutch archive states that western New Guinea initially remained under Dutch administration. Present national boundaries would misrepresent the scope of the 1949 transfer. This is an archive’s retrospective account rather than an account from Papuan communities.
rubric.chronology_geography: The Jakarta proclamation and The Hague settlement have distinct locators; neither is a point for every conflict in the archipelago.
rubric.perspective: The Dutch military label for its offensives is attributed and interrogated beside the Indonesian proclamation; neither institution speaks for every resident.
rubric.reading: The three verbs used in deeper reading give a way to remember different institutional actions.
rubric.activity: Sorting three event cards and locating the two signatures can be completed from the supplied illustration and text.
rubric.connections: Ghana provides a comparison of movements and changes in government, with different colonial institutions, struggles and territorial outcomes.

rubric.orientation: A Ghana overprint on a Gold Coast stamp makes a constitutional puzzle visible.
rubric.explanation: Organizing, elections, ministerial power, independence and the later republic explain how different powers changed at different moments.
rubric.evidence: The study describes the 1958 law as empowering the prime minister to detain certain persons without trial. This retrospective account supports the distinction between independence and political freedom. The parliamentary PDF host separately returned HTTP 403 during this review.
rubric.chronology_geography: 1957 independence and the 1960 republic help explain a royal portrait on the stamp. The deeper account explicitly reaches 1964 to discuss later restrictions.
rubric.perspective: Nkrumah’s program, regional opponents and the country study retain separate vantage points. This selection still relies on indirect accounts of market women and British Togoland/Ewe experiences.
rubric.reading: A learner can read the stamp first, then use the two differently dated accounts to ask who benefited from cocoa income.
rubric.activity: The two-column task asks for visible words, portrait and work scene first, then a separately supported explanation of the monarchy.
rubric.connections: The regional comparison distinguishes transferred powers and obligations from lived benefits. The present selection does not resolve local disagreements about the Togoland plebiscite.
